passage:
In the maths test, Sachin saw his close friend Saurabh copy from the boy in front. That night he made a list: friendship, fairness to the others, his own honesty. None of them cancelled the others. The trouble was real, and he did not yet know what to do.

Noor had seen her friend Tanvi do the same in Hindi. She caught Tanvi after school. "It worried me, seeing that. What happened?" Tanvi said she had panicked and not studied. Noor said, "Would you tell the teacher yourself? I'll go with you." Tanvi took two days, then did.

Rohit, in the back row, saw a friend copying every week. "Not my business," he told himself. The friend's marks crept above those of students who had worked hard, and each time the results were read out, Rohit's stomach turned.

Sachin, meanwhile, learned that Saurabh's parents expected top marks and checked every paper. That did not change his mind: the copying had to stop. But it changed how he went about it. He told Saurabh so, and then went with him to ask the teacher about extra tutoring.

qa.q: Whom did Sachin see copying?
qa.a: Sachin saw his close friend Saurabh copy.

qa.q: How did Noor's response to a copying friend differ from Rohit's, and what followed?
qa.a: Noor spoke to Tanvi privately and gave her a chance to tell the teacher, and Tanvi did, while Rohit told himself it was not his business, the friend's marks crept above hard workers' marks, and Rohit felt uneasy each time.

qa.q: What might Saurabh be feeling under pressure from home?
qa.a: Fear of disappointing the parents, which pushes Saurabh to copy.

qa.q: What could Rohit do now?
qa.a: Rohit could speak to his friend privately, or tell a teacher, rather than only watching.

grounding: Four approaches to a friend who cheats: weighing loyalty and honesty, talking first, staying silent, and rethinking after learning the friend's reasons.

passage:
Last year Pallavi, then a third-year, wanted to be the helpful mentor for Aparna. Whenever Aparna got stuck, Pallavi typed the solution. Aparna nodded, thanked her, and came back the next day with the next problem. By the exams she could not write a loop alone.

This year, as a final-year student, Pallavi met a new junior, Naveen, and began differently. "What do you actually want?" she asked. "A first internship," he said. So instead of describing her own path, she looked at what internships asked for.

She broke "learn programming" down week by week: one concept, one exercise, one small program. Every Saturday they went over Naveen's work together, and Pallavi asked "what would you try?" before she said anything.

One Saturday Naveen asked about machine learning. Pallavi laughed. "I don't know it well enough to advise you. But a senior in that area is in the lab on Mondays. I'll introduce you." Naveen looked relieved that she had said it plainly.

qa.q: What did Naveen say he wanted?
qa.a: Naveen said he wanted a first internship.

qa.q: How did Pallavi's mentoring of Naveen differ from her earlier mentoring of Aparna, and what were the results?
qa.a: With Aparna she typed every solution, so Aparna could not write a loop alone, while with Naveen she asked what he wanted, set small weekly steps and asked what he would try first.

qa.q: What was Naveen feeling when Pallavi said she did not know machine learning well enough?
qa.a: Relief and trust, since she said it plainly and offered a real introduction.

qa.q: What could Pallavi do when Naveen is stuck next week?
qa.a: Pallavi could ask what he has tried and give a hint rather than the whole answer.

grounding: Four approaches to mentoring a junior: starting with their goal, small weekly steps, solving everything for them, and referring on when out of depth.

passage:
Before trying for a baby, Indu and Nilesh sat with tea and a notebook. When would they start? Who would take leave, and how would it work? What would change in what they spent? They wrote answers together instead of guessing at each other's.

Then Indu read the company's rules on maternity and paternity leave and worked out how many months her income would shrink. For a year they put a little aside each month, so a cushion would be waiting.

One thing they never asked. Both simply took for granted that Nilesh's parents would come and live with them to help. When the baby was two months away, Nilesh's father, Lalit, said kindly that his knees and their home made it hard to move. The couple had no plan, and spent a frantic week phoning relatives.

After the first month, Indu was grey with tiredness: she had taken every night. They tried alternate nights and hired a part-time helper in the daytime. Every evening they asked each other, "How are you really doing?"

qa.q: Who said that moving in would be hard?
qa.a: Nilesh's father, Lalit, said it.

qa.q: Why did the couple scramble over childcare even though they had planned leave and money carefully?
qa.a: They discussed leave and savings but never asked Nilesh's parents, simply taking for granted they would move in, so they had no plan when Lalit said it was hard.

qa.q: What was Indu feeling after the first month?
qa.a: Exhausted and probably overwhelmed after taking every night.

qa.q: What could the couple do next?
qa.a: They could keep the alternate nights and part-time help, and check in each evening about how each is coping.

grounding: Four approaches to planning for a baby: a joint talk on timing and roles, checking leave and saving, assuming grandparent help, and reviewing after the birth.

passage:
Three children spotted the jar of sweets on the top shelf.

Vijay went straight to the kitchen door. "Papa, can you get the jar down?" he said, pointing. His father lifted it down, gave each child one, and put it back.

Deepak rose onto his toes, arms straight up, and stretched. He stretched again and pulled at the air. "If I try hard, my arms will get long," Deepak said. The jar stayed where it was.

Tushar had a different plan. He hauled a chair over to the cupboard and climbed on it. Still too short. He fetched a stool and put it on the chair. Halfway up, the whole stack began to wobble. Tushar's tummy dropped. He climbed down at once and shouted, "Mama! Come, please!" Mama came running, steadied the chair, and took the jar down herself.

qa.q: What did Tushar put on the chair?
qa.a: Tushar put a stool on the chair.

qa.q: How did Vijay's way of reaching the jar differ from Tushar's, and which was safer?
qa.a: Vijay asked his father, which was quick and safe, while Tushar stacked a stool on a chair and it wobbled until he climbed down and called for help.

qa.q: What was Tushar feeling when the stack wobbled?
qa.a: Fear, since his tummy dropped and he climbed down at once.

qa.q: What could Deepak try instead of stretching?
qa.a: Deepak could look at how far the jar is and ask a grown-up to get it.

grounding: Four approaches to reaching something high: stacking furniture, asking an adult, wishing arms longer, and stopping when the stack wobbles.

passage:
At ten past four on a Thursday, Gopika ran a cleanup command and watched the customer table vanish. Her hands went cold. Within minutes she messaged her lead, Afreen: "I deleted the customer table by mistake. Here is the command, the time, and the records it touched."

Afreen asked, "What might still go wrong?" Gopika stopped the nightly job before it could copy the empty table, then restored the data from last night's backup. By evening the affected customers had a plain message saying what had happened and when their data would be back. The blame talk could wait until morning.

Suraj had been through a slip of his own last spring. He had quietly fixed a wrong figure in a report and said nothing. Six months later an audit found the change. The mistake had been small; the hiding was what made the team stop trusting his sign-offs.

Gopika spent the next months finishing tasks when she said she would and warning early when a date would slip. She wrote short updates without being asked. By winter Afreen handed her the billing migration again.

qa.q: What did Gopika do before restoring the data?
qa.a: She stopped the nightly job.

qa.q: How did Suraj's way of handling his mistake differ from Gopika's, and what was the effect on trust?
qa.a: Suraj quietly fixed his error and said nothing, and when the audit found it the team stopped trusting his sign-offs, while Gopika told her lead within minutes and rebuilt trust with steady updates.

qa.q: What was Gopika feeling when the table vanished?
qa.a: Alarm and dread, shown by her cold hands.

qa.q: What could Suraj do to rebuild trust?
qa.a: Suraj could own the earlier slip openly, then deliver on time and warn early about delays.

grounding: Four approaches to a major work mistake: disclosing quickly, containing damage first, hiding it, and rebuilding trust with small reliable deliveries.

passage:
Yusuf and Chandrika both grabbed the toy car on Monday, and both shouted. Chandrika ran to the teacher, who crouched down and listened to each of them in turn, then helped them agree: Yusuf first, Chandrika after the song.

On Tuesday it was the red truck. Yusuf gripped it. Chandrika took a breath and said, "You have it now, I have it after lunch." Yusuf thought about it and let out a big sigh. "Okay." The shouting stopped, and each got a turn.

On Wednesday, when they both wanted the drum, Yusuf turned his back and stared at the wall as though nothing was happening. His face was tight. Chandrika looked at his back, puzzled, and did not know if he was still her friend.

On Thursday they reached for the same crayon. Jomon, watching, said, "Toss a coin. Heads is Yusuf, tails is Chandrika." They both nodded, and it landed on tails. On Friday, at the next squabble, Yusuf said, "Let's toss a coin!" and dug out the coin himself.

qa.q: What did the teacher do before helping them agree?
qa.a: The teacher crouched down and listened to each of them in turn.

qa.q: How did Yusuf's silent turning away differ from Chandrika's bargaining, and what did each do to the quarrel?
qa.a: Chandrika named a fair split of time, which ended the shouting with a turn each, while Yusuf turned his back and left the hurt in place, and Chandrika was puzzled by the silence.

qa.q: What was Chandrika feeling when Yusuf turned his back?
qa.a: Puzzled and a bit worried that they were no longer friends.

qa.q: How could a teacher help Yusuf when he turns away?
qa.a: A teacher could sit with him, ask what he wanted, and help him tell Chandrika.

grounding: Four ways young children settle a quarrel: asking an adult, bargaining, ignoring it, and copying a peer's coin toss.
